where: Section 2 (last paragraph), worked example step 4, exam trap 2
problem: The chapter says that without FormsModule the input 'stays a dumb box', the class field silently never changes and totals 'show blank'. That is not what Angular does. When [(ngModel)] or [ngModel] appears in a template whose component (or NgModule) does not import FormsModule, Angular fails to compile the template and throws the error 'Can't bind to ngModel since it isn't a known property of input' (NG8002). Nothing renders silently blank; the page breaks or the build fails.
fix: State the real consequence: [(ngModel)] is unknown to Angular unless FormsModule is imported in the standalone component's imports array (or the NgModule's imports), and the template then fails to compile with the ngModel-not-a-known-property error. Only with schemas: [NO_ERRORS_SCHEMA] (not recommended) would the box accept typing with no effect on the class field.

problem: The answer is wrong and self-contradictory. It says Angular 'binds that function as the handler' and then that 'it is called without arguments'. Angular does not call it: (click)="save" is evaluated as a statement, which merely reads the property save and returns the method reference; that value is ignored and the method never runs. The click does nothing and no error is shown. Saying a parameter 'receives undefined' implies the method does run, which it does not.
fix: Answer: the statement is just the expression save, a property read that returns the method reference; Angular does not invoke it, so the handler never runs and the click looks dead (no error is thrown). Writing (click)="save()" calls it with no arguments, and (click)="save($event)" or (click)="save(item)" passes the event or a value explicitly.

problem: The listed template has the name line, the price line, the Total line and 'Add', but the two bindings that the later steps depend on are never shown: the input using [(ngModel)]="qty" and the button's (click)="add.emit(product)". Steps 4 and 6 refer to markup the student cannot see.
fix:
Show the full template, for example:

{{ product.name | uppercase }}

{{ product.price | currency:'INR' }}

Total: {{ product.price * qty | currency:'INR' }}

.

problem: 'Passes 2499 through the currency pipe with the Indian rupee locale' is inaccurate. The pipe keeps the application's locale (en-US by default) and only takes the currency code INR from the argument. The value happens to look the same here, but a student may expect Indian digit grouping; in the en-US locale 249900 rupees prints ₹249,900.00, while a registered en-IN locale prints ₹2,49,900.00.
fix: Say: the pipe formats the number in the app's current locale (default en-US: comma every three digits, dot as decimal) using the INR symbol ₹ and two decimals, giving ₹2,499.00 and ₹7,497.00. Add that registering the en-IN locale changes grouping to the lakh/crore style.

problem: 'Typing 3 writes 3 into the class field qty' is only true if the input is type="number". A plain text input bound with ngModel writes the string "3", which is why 2499 * qty still gives 7497 by JavaScript number coercion. A student adding qty to price instead would get string concatenation, not addition.
fix: Say: typing 3 into <input type="number" [(ngModel)]="qty"> writes the number 3 into qty. Note that a text input would write the string "3", so the total still works for multiplication but breaks for addition.

problem: '*ngFor over a list without trackBy rebuilds every row on each change' overstates it. The default trackBy is object identity, so rows whose item reference has not changed are reused; rows are re-created when the item references change (for example, fresh objects returned by an API call).
fix: Say: without trackBy, Angular matches rows by object identity, so a new array of new objects makes Angular throw away and rebuild every row, losing input focus and animations. Supplying a trackBy that returns a stable id (p.id, not the index) lets Angular move existing rows instead.

where: Exam traps, property versus attribute bullet
problem: 'colspan is an HTML attribute with no matching DOM property' is not quite right. The table cell DOM property exists but is camelCase: HTMLTableCellElement.colSpan. Angular property binding is case-sensitive, so [colspan] fails while [colSpan] works; [attr.colspan] also works. As written, a student may think no property exists at all.
fix: Say: colspan is an attribute whose DOM property is spelled colSpan; Angular's property binding matches property names exactly, so [colspan] finds nothing and fails, while [colSpan]="cols" and the always-safe [attr.colspan]="cols" both work. Use attr. binding for attribute-only names such as aria-label.

problem: @angular/flex-layout is deprecated and no longer maintained, so presenting fxLayout and fxFlex as current practice is misleading for students reading new job-oriented material.
fix: Keep it as legacy: 'Older projects use Flex-Layout directives such as fxLayout="row" and fxFlex; the package is deprecated, so newer code writes this layout in plain CSS (flexbox or grid).'
